title: LEFT, RIGHT, MID and LEN
explanation: A shipping company packs 3 facts into each order code: the city, the year and the order number, like **NYC-2026-0457**. To analyse orders by city or year, you need those pieces in their own columns. LEFT, RIGHT and MID pull out part of a piece of text by position.

tasks.prompt: In B2, pull out the city: the first 3 characters. Use =LEFT(A2, 3).
tasks.teach: **LEFT(text, n)** takes the first **n** characters from the left. So `=LEFT("NYC-2026-0457", 3)` gives NYC.
hints: The city is the first 3 characters.

tasks.prompt: In D2, pull out the order number: the last 4 characters. Use RIGHT.
tasks.teach: **RIGHT(text, n)** takes the last **n** characters. The result is text, so a leading zero like 0457 is kept.
hints: RIGHT works like LEFT, from the other end.

tasks.prompt: In C2, pull out the year from the middle: =MID(A2, 5, 4).
tasks.teach: **MID(text, start, n)** takes **n** characters starting at position **start**. Count the characters: N=1, Y=2, C=3, -=4, so the year starts at position **5** and is 4 characters long.
hints: The year starts at character 5 and is 4 characters long.

tasks.prompt: Copy B2:D2 down to row 6, so every order is split up.
hints: Select B2:D2, copy, select B3:D6, paste.

tasks.prompt: Last one: in E2, count the characters in the code with LEN, then copy it down to E6. Every code should have the same length, which is a quick way to spot a typo.
tasks.answer: =LEN(A2) in E2, then copy down to E6

recap: LEFT takes characters from the start, RIGHT from the end, and MID from any position. LEN counts characters, which helps you check codes are the right length.
